messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Vignette:
Kwame is an 18-year-old African American young man who recently began working as a tax consultant, one of the youngest people in his office and, until the past year, proud of how quickly he had moved into a professional environment. When he speaks about the assault, he does so in fragments, as if the memory comes to him first in flashes rather than as a full story. He remembers being raped by a man when he was alone with him, and what stays with him most sharply are particular sensory moments: the sudden sound of shouting, the noise of a door opening and then slamming, and the immediate realization that there was no one else there. In the memory, those sounds seem to fill the whole space. He can still bring back isolated visual images from the assault with disturbing clarity, like snapshots he did not choose to keep. At other times there is no picture at all, only the same overwhelming fear and helplessness crashing over him without warning. He says that when this happens he can even taste what he tasted during the rape, as if his body has been pulled back into that moment before his mind has caught up.

In the weeks afterward, Kwame found himself reacting to ordinary situations as though they might turn dangerous at any second. If someone touched him unexpectedly, even lightly on the shoulder, he would jolt hard and feel a burst of alarm before he could tell himself where he was. He became acutely alert to men around him, especially if he might end up alone with one. What frightened him most was not just remembering what had happened, but the sense that it could happen again if he failed to notice danger quickly enough. He had come to believe that unfamiliar places were especially unsafe because he could not judge exits, other people, or what might happen behind a closed door. As a result, he began restricting himself to routes and settings he already knew.

This has shaped how he moves through daily life. At work, he is expected to meet clients and consult with colleagues in offices and conference rooms, but certain ordinary moments are hard for him to get through. A door opening suddenly behind him, or a nearby office door slamming shut, can send a shock through his body before he has registered that it is only someone arriving late to a meeting. If a male coworker asks to speak with him alone, Kwame feels his chest tighten and his attention narrow to where the man is standing, how close he is, and where the door is. He tries to keep interactions brief or position himself so he is not trapped in the room. When new assignments require him to go somewhere unfamiliar, he hesitates or looks for reasons to delay. To him this feels sensible rather than excessive; if he does not know the place, he cannot assess the danger, and that uncertainty feels intolerable.

Outside work, strangers approaching him in ordinary settings feel threatening in a way he knows other people do not seem to understand. A man stepping toward him to ask a question on the sidewalk or in a store can make him brace immediately, his body preparing before he has decided whether the person means harm. He avoids unfamiliar neighborhoods and social situations, especially if he cannot predict who will be there. Over time this has narrowed his life. Being single has come to feel less like a neutral fact and more like part of the distance he keeps around himself. He goes where he needs to go, then comes home.

What stands out in session is how often the assault returns to him through sensory pieces rather than a full narrative. Sometimes he sees it in pictures; sometimes there is only the emotion, sudden and complete; sometimes the taste comes first and he feels instantly revolted and terrified, as if the present has dropped away. He does not describe these episodes as memories at first. They feel too immediate for that. He says the worst moments are when something as ordinary as shouting in the hallway at work, a door banging, or being alone with a man makes it feel as though his body already knows something terrible is about to happen.

Kwame is seeking help now because the effort of managing all this has started to collide with the life he is trying to build. He wants to keep his job and function like the competent young professional others assume he is, but he is exhausted by how much of each day is organized around staying alert and staying away. He is most afraid of being caught off guard again, especially in a closed room with a man he does not know well. At the same time, he hopes treatment might make it possible for him to be in ordinary places, hear ordinary sounds, and not feel as though he has been thrown back into the assault.
